summary: KGM's first electric SUV for Australia arrives as a single fully-equipped front-drive grade carrying the largest battery in its price class - 80.6kWh of BYD LFP Blade - but Australian reviewers agree that battery buys less range than it should, with a 462km WLTP claim that trails the smaller-batteried Geely EX5 and testers recording between 18.2 and 21.7kWh/100km. Where they part company is whether the fundamentals compensate: CarsGuide scored it 7.1/10 for interfaces that simply work and a genuinely roomy cabin, while CarExpert and The Driven both flagged missing equipment for the money and 339Nm regularly overwhelming the front tyres. The counterweight is running cost - $2,114 of capped-price servicing over seven years and an unconditional seven-year warranty - set against no ANCAP rating at all and just 168 Torres of any kind sold in Australia across the whole first half of 2025.
pros: Capped-price servicing totals $2,114 over seven years/140,000km (about $302 a year) with a complimentary first service inside six months or 5,000km, and KGM's seven-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional - you may service outside the KGM dealer network provided you keep records proving the work met KGM's specification - while the BYD Blade pack carries a separate 10-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty guaranteeing at least 70 per cent state of health

The 80.6kWh battery is the biggest in the sub-$60,000 mid-size electric SUV class - Geely EX5 68.4kWh, MG S5 62kWh, BYD Atto 3 60.5kWh - and it supports 3.5kW vehicle-to-load, 120-130kW DC charging (10-80 per cent in about 37 minutes) and 10.5kW three-phase AC
1,500kg braked towing where the Geely EX5 is not rated to tow at all and the MG S5 and BYD Atto 3 stop at 750kg, plus a 465-litre boot that opens out to 1,526 litres with the rear seats folded

One grade, no options list to navigate and no cheaper trim that deletes equipment: 18-inch alloys, powered sunroof, twin 12.3-inch screens, synthetic leather, heated and ventilated front seats, 360-degree camera, eight airbags and full driver-assist including lane centring and junction-assist AEB are all standard

A $5,010 factory bonus off the recommended retail price was running at the research date, taking the car to $53,690 drive-away with metallic paint included - available for a limited time and while stocks last, so it is a buying-window discount rather than a permanent repositioning
cons: 462km WLTP from 80.6kWh is the weakest efficiency in the class - the Geely EX5 gets 475km from 68.4kWh - and CarExpert measured 21.7kWh/100km against the 18.7kWh/100km claim; worse, 462km is the identical figure KGM published for the superseded 73.4kWh pack while Europe rates the 80.6kWh car at 503km, so the Australian range claim may simply be a carried-over number

No ANCAP rating at all, and no KGM or SsangYong model is ANCAP-rated, so a fleet or salary-packaging buyer with a five-star purchasing policy cannot order one despite the eight airbags and full driver-assist suite

Front-wheel drive only with no AWD option offered, and CarsGuide, CarExpert and The Driven independently report the 339Nm overwhelming the front Nexen tyres off the line, with regenerative braking that feels inconsistent

KGM sold 168 Torres in the first half of 2025 against 24,034 Toyota RAV4s, and the brand's total 2025 Australian volume of 4,116 was down 23.7 per cent - thin dealer coverage, and a $5,010 factory bonus on new stock pushes used values down further; CarsGuide's own verdict is that rivals come 'from brands that might hold their value better'

No spare wheel (a repair kit only), climate control is touchscreen-only so you must leave CarPlay to change the temperature, and there is no built-in navigation, no wireless phone mirroring and no wireless charging pad - a cable is mandatory
